props.title: The Cat's Meow

sections.content: Peter Bogdanovich's The Cat's Meow dives into one of Hollywood's most infamous unsolved mysteries - the 1924 death of producer Thomas Ince aboard William Randolph Hearst's yacht. Like Bogdanovich's earlier The Last Picture Show (1971), it peels back glamour to reveal raw human drama. The film joins other piercing looks at early Hollywood like Chaplin (1992) and Hollywoodland (2006), exposing the dark underbelly of the nascent film industry's golden age.

sections.content: The film captures 1920s Hollywood's decadence through meticulous period detail and a stellar ensemble cast. Edward Herrmann embodies Hearst's paranoid power, while Kirsten Dunst brings surprising depth to Marion Davies, often unfairly reduced to a punchline in Citizen Kane (1941). Like Sunset Boulevard (1950) and The Artist (2011), it shows how Hollywood's magic factory could destroy the very people who created it.

Bogdanovich's insider knowledge of Hollywood history enriches every frame. Having personally known Orson Welles and other golden age figures, he brings authenticity to this Jazz Age tragedy. The film pairs naturally with Mank (2020) and Once Upon a Time in Hollywood (2019) in examining pivotal moments when the movie industry's innocence collided with brutal reality. sections.content: While The Cat's Meow focuses on one infamous weekend, it reflects broader themes of power, celebrity, and corruption that defined early Hollywood. Similar territory is explored in Cafe Society (2016) and L.A. Confidential (1997), where the movie industry's glamorous surface masks deadly serious power plays. The film's portrayal of William Randolph Hearst particularly resonates with later media mogul stories like The Social Network (2010) and Citizen Kane (1941) itself.
